title: Who Really Pays for Tariffs?
question: Who actually pays for tariffs, and do they raise the prices Americans pay?
alternates: Do Tariffs Raise Prices? What the 2025 Data Show
Tariffs: Do Foreign Exporters Pay, or Do We?
premise: Foreign exporters absorbed little of the 2025 tariffs: US importers bore about 94% of the incidence from January to August 2025 and 86% by November, according to New York Fed import-price regressions. Of a tariff increase, about 26% reached consumer goods prices within a year, and not at once: about half of the direct effect is in shop prices after three months and all of it by six, while surveyed firms describe fixed-price contracts and deliberately gradual increases, so retailers do not reprice the moment a tariff is announced. About a third of the consumer price effect came through domestically made goods, as US producers paid more for imported inputs and faced less competition. These are estimates relative to less-exposed goods, covering goods only, and they leave out the exchange rate and monetary policy. Over time the tariff effect raised the goods price level by close to 3% at its February 2026 peak and stays positive, while its contribution to twelve-month inflation is forecast to fade, so tariffs look like a rise in the level of prices more than lasting inflation; but business surveys find firms spreading increases over long periods, so in practice the one-time rise is drawn out, especially when tariffs keep changing.
whyWatch: Politicians say foreign countries pay the tariffs; critics say consumers do. New York Fed research on the 2025 tariffs measured where the cost actually landed and how much reached store shelves.
tension: If foreign exporters cut their prices to keep selling, Americans pay nothing extra. If they do not, the cost lands on US importers and then on shoppers, including for goods made at home.

arc.hook: A tariff is a tax paid at the US border. The fight is over who ends up carrying it.
arc.conflict: One side says foreign exporters cut their prices and eat the cost; the other says Americans pay it all at the checkout.
arc.evidence: The New York Fed's incidence estimates, then the pass-through to consumer prices for imported and domestic goods, then the price level against the inflation rate over time.
arc.resolution: US importers paid most of the 2025 tariffs, and part of that cost reached consumer prices, including for goods made at home. The effect raises the price level and fades from the inflation rate, but slowly.
arc.takeaway: A tariff that foreign sellers do not absorb is paid at home, by firms first and shoppers over the following year.
